paper_title: HuGe: Scaling Humanoid Generalist Vision-Language-Action Models with Egocentric Experience

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios. Although egocentric human demonstrations provide a complementary source of task experience, differences in visual embodiment and missing robot proprioception complicate transfer to humanoid policies. To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs pre-trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, HuGe employs three existing representative VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller, together with hand-control signals. Based on this, we introduce a three-stage training pipeline that combines egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning. To facilitate transfer across embodiments, we construct pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulation playback during pre-training and modify arm appearance in egocentric observations through re-rendering during downstream fine-tuning. With this pipeline, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art on simulation benchmark HumanoidArena. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 indicate that augmenting robot demonstrations with visually adapted egocentric demonstrations significantly increases success on a pick-and-drop task.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [60, 16, 7, 6, 53, 19] fueled by Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [4, 37] and World Models (WMs) [47, 1] have enabled language-conditioned manipulation across wide range of tabletop tasks. Building on this progress, extending VLAs to humanoid robots offers the potential to perform diverse tasks in human environments by combining manipulation with whole-body mobility. Despite this potential, adapting VLAs to humanoid robots remains challenging because task execution requires coordinated whole-body motion while maintaining balance and stability. To meet these control requirements, existing humanoid loco-manipulation approaches commonly employ hierarchical architectures that combine high-level policies with reinforcement learning (RL)-based controllers [13, 52, 2]. To this end, central research question is how to train generalist VLAs that translate language instructions into coordinated whole-body behaviors across diverse tasks. Realizing this goal requires addressing two key challenges. First, the high-dimensional action spaces and complex dynamics of humanoid robots make it difficult to directly transfer VLA policies developed for robotic manipulators to whole-body control. In particular, arm movements must be coordinated with the torso and lower body to accomplish Equal contribution. Corresponding authors.

sections.title: HuGe
sections.content: manipulation objectives while maintaining balance and stability. Consequently, VLA-based humanoid control requires an action interface that connects task-level predictions to coordinated whole-body execution. Second, beyond these control challenges, learning generalist humanoid behaviors requires diverse whole-body demonstrations, yet collecting such data on real-world robots is costly and time-consuming. To alleviate this data bottleneck, egocentric human demonstrations offer complementary source of task experience for large-scale training. However, differences in visual embodiment and the absence of robot proprioceptive observations complicate the direct use of these demonstrations for humanoid policy learning. These challenges motivate an approach that integrates VLA policies with whole-body control and supports effective transfer from egocentric human experience to humanoid robots through scalable training pipeline. To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs that operate through wholebody controller and learn from large-scale mixture of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, HuGe builds on existing representative VLA architectures and follows three-stage training pipeline that sequentially incorporates egocentric human data, humanoid teleoperation data, and mixture of downstream demonstrations. To support this pipeline, we assemble training corpus comprising over 2,000 hours of egocentric and robot data. Furthermore, we prepare egocentric data for humanoid policy learning during both pre-training and downstream fine-tuning. In particular, during pre-training, we use simulation playback to construct pseudo-proprioceptive states for egocentric data that lack robot proprioceptive observations. Building on this pre-training stage, we re-render and replace arm regions in egocentric observations during downstream fine-tuning. To assess the effectiveness of this approach, we compare HuGe with baseline methods on the HumanoidArena simulation benchmark and further evaluate its performance on real-world humanoid tasks. Overall, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art performance on HumanoidArena, demonstrating its capability for humanoid whole-body control, while comprehensive real-world experiments and solid analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of the training recipe. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce HuGe, family of humanoid generalist VLAs, trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data through three-stage training pipeline. We develop data adaptation methods that facilitate the transfer of egocentric human experience to humanoid policy learning. HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art performance against baselines on HumanoidArena, while comprehensive real-world experiments and analyses validate our design choices and training paradigm.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [60, 16, 7, 6] built on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [4, 37] and WorldAction Models (WAMs) [53, 19, 54] based on video-prediction World Models (WMs) [47, 1] have advanced rapidly in fixed-base single-arm and bimanual manipulation. Beyond language-conditioned task execution, these approaches combine robot demonstrations with pretrained multimodal knowledge or predictions of future observations to support policy learning across diverse manipulation tasks [45, 51, 24]. These advances have enabled robotic manipulators to autonomously fold and organize deformable objects such as clothes and towels, perform precise operations such as connector insertion and small-part assembly, and complete long-horizon tasks such as table setting and coffee preparation [33, 22, 32, 43]. For humanoid whole-body control, we adopt three representative VLA architectures, OFT [15], GR00T [6], and π [7], without introducing additional modules or modifying the architectural designs. Using these architectures, we investigate humanoid whole-body control and training strategies centered on egocentric human demonstrations, complemented by robot data for embodiment adaptation and downstream task learning. 2.2 Humanoid Whole-Body Control Early reinforcement-learning approaches to humanoid control focused on locomotion, training policies in simulation to maintain balance, follow velocity commands, and adapt to terrain variations during real-world deployment [39]. Subsequent work expanded these capabilities to whole-body motion tracking, using retargeted human motions to train controllers that support coordinated teleoperation and autonomous skill learning from demonstrations [10, 9, 29, 36]. Building on these control capabilities, one line of hierarchical VLA approaches predicts upper-body manipulation targets alongside lower-body motion commands, relying on reinforcement-learning controllers to execute locomotion and posture adjustments [23, 13, 52, 2]. Alongside this direction, advances in whole-body motion models have supported VLA and world-action approaches that generate full-body motion references or unified motion latents, which whole-body controllers translate into coordinated joint commands [58, 21]. In contrast, we focus on training strategies

sections.content: Figure 1: Schematic of the HuGe framework, architecture and training pipeline. centered on egocentric human demonstrations for humanoid whole-body control, examining three established VLA architectures without adding modules or modifying the architectural designs. 2.3 Egocentric Learning Egocentric human demonstrations provide diverse observations and complementary source of experience for robot learning. Early approaches use human videos to learn visual representations and motion priors that support downstream policy learning [31, 38, 30, 48]. Building on these efforts, more direct approaches learn action prediction from annotated human motions or inferred latent actions, incorporating human and robot data through pre-training, co-training, and task-specific adaptation [27, 20, 28, 59]. To address embodiment differences, another line of work converts human demonstrations into robot-compatible data through motion retargeting and visual adaptation, including human-arm removal, robot rendering, and embodiment masking [17, 14, 55]. Beyond fixed-base manipulation, related efforts extend human-data learning to humanoid manipulation and loco-manipulation through aligned action representations and staged training with robot demonstrations [52]. Within this setting, we investigate how egocentric human demonstrations can support humanoid whole-body policy learning through controller-compatible action supervision, simulation-derived pseudo-proprioceptive states, and visual adaptation across training stages.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.content: In this section, we present the model architecture and training recipe of HuGe, as shown in Figure 1. We first describe how three representative VLA architectures are instantiated for humanoid control. Building on these model instantiations, we introduce three-stage training pipeline that progressively incorporates egocentric human experience, humanoid demonstrations, and task-specific mixture data. 3.1 Architecture Given visual observation ot, proprioceptive state st, and natural-language task instruction l, HuGe predicts 66-dimensional action vector at for humanoid control at time step t. The action consists of 64-dimensional latent motion token and two binary variables specifying whether the left and right hands are open or closed. The motion token lies in the universal token space of SONIC [29], pretrained whole-body controller. Conditioned on the proprioceptive state of robot, control decoder of SONIC converts the predicted motion token into joint-level commands for whole-body motion, while the two binary variables separately control hand opening and closing. This interface allows HuGe to predict task-conditioned whole-body actions while relying on the low-level controller for coordinated motion execution. We instantiate HuGe with three existing representative VLA designs: OFT [15], GR00T [6], and π [7]. Across these variants, Qwen-based vision-language backbones encode visual observations, proprioceptive state and language instructions, while different action prediction modules map the resulting representations to humanoid actions [44]. Specifically, the OFT-style variant uses lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) to map the hidden states of predefined

sections.title: HuGe
sections.content: action tokens directly to continuous actions, predicting an action chunk in parallel. In contrast, the GR00T-style variant separates vision-language processing from action generation: the backbone provides contextual features, and diffusion transformer (DiT) conditions on these features through cross-attention to generate action chunks via flow matching. Compared with this use of backbone output features, the π-style variant connects DiT action expert to hidden states from multiple backbone layers through layer-wise cross-attention, progressively refining noisy action sequences into continuous action chunks. For humanoid control, all three variants use the action interface defined above, with each predicted time step containing 64-dimensional latent motion token for SONIC and two hand-control signals. 3.2 Training Recipe We train HuGe through three-stage pipeline that progressively incorporates egocentric human experience, humanoid demonstrations, and task-specific mixture data. Specifically, egocentric pre-training utilizes large-scale egocentric demonstrations to learn language-conditioned action prediction. Subsequently, during humanoid adaptation, we continue training the policy on humanoid teleoperation demonstrations to adapt action prediction to robot observations and states. Finally, downstream fine-tuning adapts the policy to target tasks using task-specific demonstrations. Table 1 summarizes the data sources and dataset sizes for each training stage. To this end, we combine human demonstrations from EgoDex [11], EgoVerse [35], and Xperience-10M [42] with simulated robot demonstrations from BEHAVIOR-1K [18], expressing heterogeneous motion supervision in the SONIC action space. Although the BEHAVIOR-1K demonstrations originate from robot simulation, we include these demonstrations into the first training stage, broadly defined here as demonstrations collected without teleoperating real-world robots. Specifically, we use SONIC motion tokens for EgoDex and construct corresponding motion supervision for EgoVerse from the Aria bimanual subset. After checking tracking validity, calibration stability, segment duration, and G1 retargeting constraints, we retain 47.08 hours of EgoVerse segments. We then encode the retained head and wrist trajectories into SONIC motion tokens with fixed lower-body standing reference. In comparison, Xperience-10M provides full-body motion references, which we convert into the reference format required by the SONIC encoder. For BEHAVIOR-1K, SONIC planner generates G1 motion from upper-body pose, base-motion, and height references. Alongside these motion tokens, we derive binary hand-control labels from hand keypoints for EgoVerse and Xperience-10M and from gripper commands for BEHAVIOR-1K, while excluding unavailable EgoDex hand-action labels from supervision. To provide robot-state inputs, we replay the motion tokens on simulated G1 using the SONIC controller in simulator; for BEHAVIOR-1K, we collect paired motion tokens and states during planner-driven execution. From these simulation records, we construct 34-dimensional pseudo-proprioceptive state comprising 29 joint angles, two hand-state entries, and the three-dimensional gravity direction expressed in the body frame. Within this representation, the hand-state entries use action-label proxies when available and retain simulated hand states for EgoDex. Finally, we train each VLA variant to predict 50-step action chunks on 50 Hz control timeline from the corresponding image, task instruction, and normalized pseudo-proprioceptive state, masking padded time steps and unavailable hand-action labels.

sections.title: HuGe
sections.content: 3.2.2 Stage 2: Humanoid Adaptation Humanoid adaptation aims to transfer the policy learned from human and simulated experience to real humanoid operation. Although egocentric pre-training provides diverse motion supervision, the visual observations and pseudoproprioceptive states can differ from those encountered by real-world robot. To address this gap, we continue training each pretrained VLA variant on real G1 demonstrations, organizing heterogeneous data sources into shared action and state interface. Specifically, for Humanoid Everyday [57], we select the G1 subset and use SONIC actions and corresponding proprioceptive states. For UniFoLM-WBT [46], we combine demonstrations collected with different hand types using SONIC motion tokens and standardized binary hand-control labels. For HIW-500 [5], we augment motion tokens with hand-control labels reconstructed from controller events, retaining each hand state until the next opening or closing event. Alongside these labels, we construct proprioceptive inputs from recorded body joint positions, observation-side hand events, and gravity directions derived from the recorded controller pivot orientation. Using this common representation, we jointly adapt the vision-language backbone and action prediction modules to real robot observations and motion supervision before downstream task fine-tuning. 3.2.3 Stage 3: Downstream Fine-Tuning Downstream fine-tuning adapts the policy to target tasks and environments. Specifically, we continue training the policy separately for HumanoidArena [50] and the real-world cola pick-and-drop task. For real-world adaptation, collecting task-specific robot demonstrations through teleoperation is costly and time-consuming. In particular, joint overheating during data collection can trigger robot shutdowns, interrupting demonstrations and raising safety concerns. To reduce reliance on robot teleoperation, we supplement robot demonstrations with egocentric human demonstrations collected using PICO 4 Ultra and trackers attached to the wrists, waist, and ankles. To incorporate these demonstrations into the shared policy interface, we pair the recordings with SONIC action supervision and obtain pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulated G1 replay. However, the visible human hands and arms introduce an appearance mismatch with robot observations. To address this mismatch, we employ the visual editing pipeline of Phantom [17] to segment and remove human hands and arms, inpaint the exposed regions, and composite rendered robotic hands into the scene. Within this pipeline, temporally smoothed hand keypoints guide robotic hand rendering, while task-specific grasp constraints and thumb-visibility prior govern hand configuration and object occlusion in the cola grasping setting. Throughout this visual transformation, the synthesized videos retain the action targets, pseudo-proprioceptive states, and task instructions associated with the original recordings. Finally, we combine the synthesized human demonstrations with real robot demonstrations for supervised task adaptation, enabling human task experience to supplement robot data under visual representation that more closely resembles robot observations.

sections.title: 4 Experimentation
sections.content: We first conduct simulation experiments to iteratively refine the training strategy and egocentric pre-training recipe for humanoid VLAs. Specifically, experiments on HumanoidArena examine training strategies, the effectiveness of pseudoproprioceptive states during pre-training, and the scale of egocentric pre-training data. Building on these investigations, we then explore downstream fine-tuning and task adaptation on the real-world Unitree G1 robot, focusing on the composition of robot and egocentric demonstrations and the visual adaptation of egocentric observations. Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix A. 4.1 Simulation Evaluation We evaluate HuGe on seven HumanoidArena tasks [50]: three Human-Object Interaction (HOI) tasks and four HumanScene Interaction (HSI) tasks. Using monocular egocentric RGB observations, language instructions, and robot proprioceptive states, we train multitask policy for each variant in one run with 100 demonstrations per task. We then evaluate 60 episodes per task (three seed groups of 20), sharing task configurations across variants. Finally, we report task success rates, and unweighted task averages for HOI, HSI, and all seven tasks. 4.1.1 Training Strategy We first investigate which training strategy is most effective for learning humanoid VLAs. To this end, we compare frozen-backbone training (Frozen), low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [12], and full-parameter fine-tuning (Full) across the three HuGe variants on HumanoidArena. As shown in Table 2, LoRA achieves higher performance than frozen-backbone training for all three variants, supporting the value of backbone adaptation in this setting. However, full-parameter fine-tuning yields further improvements, achieving average success rates of 55.00%, 58.33%, and 60.24% for HuGe-OFT, HuGe-GR00T, and HuGe-Pi, respectively, and exceeding LoRA by 19.2938.81 percentage

However, egocentric human demonstrations lack the corresponding robot-state information. To assess whether pseudo-proprioceptive states can compensate for this missing input during large-scale egocentric pre-training, we compare the three HuGe variants with and without pseudo-proprioceptive states during the egocentric pre-training stage. As shown in Table 3, incorporating these states improves average success rate by 5.00 and 2.86 percentage points for HuGe-GR00T and HuGe-Pi, respectively, suggesting that simulated body configurations provide useful context for learning humanoid action mappings from human demonstrations. More specifically, SitSofa success increases from 61.67% to 78.33% and from 68.33% to 83.33%, respectively, consistent with the potential value of body-state information for tasks involving substantial posture changes. In contrast, HuGe-OFT decreases from 56.43% to 54.05%. This degradation is associated with the textual state interface. Specifically, proprioceptive states are serialized as text, and input truncation leaves incomplete state descriptions that introduce ambiguity into action prediction. sections.title: HuGe
sections.content: 4.1.4 Performance Comparison To put our results in perspective, we compare the three HuGe variants to number of baselines on HumanoidArena. Specifically, Table 4 includes ACT [56], DP [8], FM [3], and π0.5 [34] results reported in the original HumanoidArena study [50]. Additionally, we evaluate GR00T [6] baselines trained from scratch or initialized from GR00T N1.7. Overall, HuGe-GR00T and HuGe-Pi achieve average success rates of 66.67% and 65.00%, respectively, exceeding the strongest baseline, π0.5, by 12.86 and 11.19 percentage points. Moreover, both variants outperform all listed baselines in the HOI and HSI averages, indicating that the overall gains extend across both interaction categories. Meanwhile, HuGe-OFT achieves lower overall average of 54.05% but leads on Boxing and VisNavi with 73.33% success on each task, showing that the strongest overall variant does not dominate every task. However, all three variants achieve success rates between 0% and 15.00% on DoubleDesk. This limited performance may be related to the prevalence of demonstrations containing repeated grasping attempts and the emphasis on whole-body humanoid data during pre-training. To address this limitation, future work could incorporate large-scale robotic arm manipulation data into pre-training to improve fine-grained grasping. Table 4: Main results on HumanoidArena. We evaluate HuGe on cola pick-and-drop task using Unitree G1 equipped with Inspire dexterous hands, as shown in Figure 3(a). Specifically, the robot must approach table, pick up bottle, turn and walk toward bin, and crouch to place the bottle inside. By combining locomotion, grasping, and object placement, this task is designed to assess coordinated whole-body control over long-horizon sequence. Furthermore, we randomize the bottle position on the tabletop to assess generalization, as illustrated in Figure 3(b). For these real-world experiments, we use only the π-style architecture of HuGe. To assess the contribution of egocentric data, we compare fine-tuning on 110 robot demonstrations alone with augmentation using 400 raw or visually adapted egocentric demonstrations. For each configuration, we conduct 30 trials and report the success rate as the fraction of trials that complete the full task. 4.2.1 Visual Adaptation During downstream fine-tuning, we augment egocentric human demonstrations with pseudo-proprioceptive states similar to the pre-training. Beyond these state inputs, we address prominent visual discrepancy between human and robot observations caused by differences in hand and arm appearance. Specifically, we remove the visible human hands and arms, inpaint the exposed regions, and composite simulation-rendered robotic hands into the videos while preserving the original action, state, and language supervision. Figure 4 illustrates corresponding frames before and after visual adaptation, illustrating the replacement of human hands and arms with rendered robotic counterparts. To quantify the resulting visual changes, we compare the Fréchet distance (FD) from raw and visually adapted egocentric feature distributions to real robot feature distributions. Specifically, visual adaptation reduces FD from 2.0311 to 1.3499 (33.54%) for Wan2.2 [47], from 7.5697 to 5.5204 (27.07%) for VideoMAE V2 [49], and from 305.5143 to 263.2697 (13.83%) for V-JEPA 2 [1]. These reductions indicate that visually adapted egocentric observations more closely resemble real robot observations across all three evaluated feature spaces. Consistently, Figure 5 shows synthesized features shifting toward the real robot distributions, providing complementary qualitative evidence of reduced visual discrepancy.

At the task level, Figure 3(d) reports 20 successful completions across 30 trials, with bottle pickup accounting for five of the ten failed trials and representing the largest source of failure. During deployment, we observed balance instability during bottle grasping, which we attribute in part to the weight of the dexterous hands. This instability contributes to unsuccessful grasp attempts and highlights the physical challenge of maintaining balance during manipulation. Finally, Figure 3(e) presents three execution sequences under different task conditions. Specifically, the first sequence includes deliberate perturbation absent from the fine-tuning data: the bottle is knocked over during grasping. Meanwhile, the second and third sequences use different bottle positions on the tabletop. These demonstrations provide qualitative evidence of adaptability to object disturbances and spatial generalization across the evaluated bottle placements.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented HuGe, family of humanoid VLAs trained on egocentric human and robot demonstrations through three-stage pipeline. Building on established VLA architectures and pretrained whole-body controller, HuGe incorporates pseudo-proprioceptive states and visual adaptation to support human-to-humanoid transfer. Experiments on HumanoidArena and real-world G1 pick-and-drop task support the value of egocentric human experience for whole-body policy learning. AI Use Statement The authors wrote and iteratively revised the manuscript, using generative AI tools, primarily GPT 6 Astra, to assist with wording and language polishing throughout the writing process. Additionally, Claude Opus 4.1, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Fable 5, GPT 5.4, GPT 5.5, GPT 5.6 Sol, and GPT 6 Astra assisted with implementing specific functionality according to project requirements via vibe coding defined by the authors. For schematic illustration, AI assistance was limited to generating the Ego and Tele-op data-collection illustrations in Stage 3 of Figure 1. Beyond these assistance tasks, generative AI was not used to formulate research questions or hypotheses, design the methodology or experiments, or interpret the results. The authors take full responsibility for the final manuscript and associated research artifacts, including AI-assisted text, code, and illustrations. Ethics Statement All human demonstrations newly collected for this work were provided by the authors. For physical safety during real-world robot experiments, suspension safety frame was used to provide fall protection. Additionally, we will provide data processing scripts for the existing datasets without directly redistributing the processed data. Reproducibility Statement The main paper and appendices document the experimental setup to support reimplementation and verification of the reported results. Specifically, Section 3 describes the model architectures, action representations, data sources and processing procedures, and three-stage training pipeline. Complementing these descriptions, Appendix provides training hyperparameters, hardware configurations, image preprocessing, and downstream data sampling, while Appendix specifies the proprioceptive state representation and normalization. In addition, Section 4 describes the HumanoidArena and real-world evaluation settings, episode and trial counts, and success-rate computation, with the corresponding task instructions provided in Appendix C.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: All HuGe variants use pretrained Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct [37] as the vision-language backbone. Under full-parameter fine-tuning, we jointly update the backbone, projection layers, and action modules, while keeping the SONIC controller fixed. For distributed training, we use DeepSpeed [41, 40] on single node equipped with eight NVIDIA 4090 GPUs,

sections.title: HuGe
sections.content: each with 48 GB of memory. With this setup, Stage 1 and Stage 2 training take approximately 38 and 12 hours, respectively. Detailed configurations are provided in Table 5. Table 5: Training hyper-parameters of HuGe. Specifically, RGB frames are downsampled when necessary to limit the longer side to 512 pixels while preserving the aspect ratio, padded with black pixels to form centered square, and resized to 256 256 using bicubic interpolation. During training, we randomly crop 243 243 region, corresponding to approximately 95% of each spatial dimension, and resize the crop back to 256 256 using bicubic interpolation. Additionally, we apply brightness, contrast, and saturation jitter sequentially, with factors sampled uniformly from [0.7, 1.3], [0.6, 1.4], and [0.5, 1.5], respectively. At inference, we replace random cropping with center cropping and disable color jitter. Finally, the resulting RGB images are passed to the Qwen3-VL processor to construct the visual model inputs. Across the three real-world configurations, the robot demonstrations remain fixed. For the two configurations augmented with egocentric demonstrations, raw and visually adapted videos share the same action, state, and language supervision. In both augmented configurations, robot and egocentric sample starts receive equal expected sampling probability. Additionally, all three configurations share normalization statistics computed from the preceding training data and both downstream robot and egocentric demonstrations.
